title: The One With Five Steaks And An Eggplant

jokes.text: Ross watching Spanish midget wrestling while pining over Julie — his channel-surfing leads him to accidentally say Julie's name aloud
jokes.setup: Ross is clearly heartbroken over Julie; the TV is on showing something random in the background
jokes.punchline: He says 'Spanish midgets. Spanish midgets wrestling...' then segues directly into 'Julie!' — his lovesick brain connecting absurd wrestling to his ex
jokes.explanation: Strong opener because it does double work: establishes Ross's pathetic romantic state and delivers an absurd non sequitur. The connection between Spanish midget wrestling and Julie is perfectly senseless yet Ross sells it completely earnestly. Character-specific because only sad-sack Ross would make this leap.

jokes.text: Chandler's deadpan: 'Julie! Okay, I see how you got there.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just made an inexplicable leap from Spanish midget wrestling to shouting Julie's name
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry 'Okay, I see how you got there' — sarcastically validating completely insane logic
jokes.explanation: A quintessential Chandler line — economical, dry, and perfectly timed. The sarcasm of pretending to follow logic that's completely insane is a signature Chandler move. High character integration because this exact delivery is what makes him Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't answer my phone because I'm busy. If I answered it, people would know I'm not busy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

jokes.text: Chandler's phone screening justification: 'If I always answer the phone, people will think I have no life.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is screening his calls with an answering machine
jokes.punchline: His logic for ignoring calls is that answering them would signal he has no life — the opposite of normal reasoning, and ironically he's home watching wrestling
jokes.explanation: Solid observational joke with a slight ironic twist — the implication being he does have no life, which the context of the scene confirms. Functional and clever but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jade
dialogue.line: Hey, it's me. I'm drunk and I'm naked on your couch.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: 'My God! Rodrigo never gets pinned!' — Ross genuinely invested in the Spanish midget wrestling while screening calls
jokes.setup: Ross claimed to be doing the dignified act of phone screening; the call comes in during the message
jokes.punchline: He shouts in genuine shock at the wrestling outcome — revealing he's fully absorbed in this ridiculous program
jokes.explanation: A good callback that deepens the absurdity. The specificity of 'Rodrigo' is the key comic detail — Ross knows the wrestlers by name, confirming he's been watching for a while. Escalates the opening gag effectively.

dialogue.line: Oddly specific claim about being a body double for legs only

jokes.text: Jade's voicemail builds to '...and naked.' with Ross and Chandler listening in real time
jokes.setup: A woman named Jade leaves a message for 'Bob' about rekindling something — the setup sounds romantic but fairly normal
jokes.punchline: 'I got a little drunk... and naked.' The escalating confession culminates in the naked reveal, landing as pure comic misdirection
jokes.explanation: Well-structured misdirection with a clean escalation beat. The 'What?' setup from one of the guys listening — selling the audience's anticipation — is good craft. The naked reveal earns its laugh through the pause-and-build structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what? Did you just say you had a successful phone conversation with an attractive woman?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, man. She called me back!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Called you back? That's huge! I mean, you finally got a return on your investment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What investment?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your phone! You've been paying for that thing for years!

jokes.text: Chandler asks 'What?' mid-message and Jade on tape says 'I got a little drunk... and naked.' then Ross immediately picks up: 'Bob here!'
jokes.setup: Ross has been screening calls and just heard a sexy voicemail from a woman looking for 'Bob'
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately breaks his own phone-screening rule and picks up, shouting 'Bob here!' — character revealing his horniness overrides all pretense
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect joke. The setup (phone screening to seem like you have a life) is immediately obliterated by the punchline (picking up the moment a sexy woman calls). The two-word punchline 'Bob here!' is maximally economical. It pays off the screening bit, reveals character, and gets a huge laugh. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's what I'm gonna do. I'm gonna pretend I don't like her, then when she least expects it, I'll suddenly act interested. She'll be so confused, she'll have no choice but to fall for me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, that's not a plan, that's just being Chandler.

jokes.text: Jade's legs on the James Bond poster
jokes.setup: Ross calls Jade back as 'Bob'; she describes her life — teaching aerobics and partying
jokes.punchline: 'And in case you wondered, those are my legs on the new James Bond poster.' — an absurdly specific flex delivered casually
jokes.explanation: A nice throwaway joke that characterizes Jade as glamorous and somewhat ditzy. The 'in case you wondered' framing is the key — nobody asked, making it funnier. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I'm pure evil. But at least I'm evil for a pathetic reason.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What reason?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wanted you to like me.

jokes.text: 'Having a phone has finally paid off'
jokes.setup: Chandler has successfully set up a date with an apparently gorgeous, exciting woman by impersonating someone else
jokes.punchline: He reduces the whole absurd victory to a banal observation about phone ownership paying off
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler deadpan — massive understatement following a wild situation. The joke works because it treats something ridiculous as if it were a mundane domestic achievement. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Can you believe Ross wants $62 for his birthday?

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: I mean, maybe it's like $6.20 and someone just added a zero?

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Or $6 and two cents that somehow became sixty-two dollars?

jokes.text: Ross calls Chandler 'Tattoo' from Fantasy Island
jokes.setup: Ross is explaining his elaborate scheme to Chandler
jokes.punchline: He addresses Chandler as 'Tattoo' — casting himself as Mr. Roarke from Fantasy Island, framing his sleazy scheme as a grand romantic fantasy
jokes.explanation: A pop-culture reference that works because it's slightly self-aggrandizing — Ross is comparing his sordid con to a romantic fantasy. The reference has an expiry date (mid-90s audiences would get it immediately) but it's deployed with enough character awareness to land.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so we can't afford to go out because of Ross's birthday dinner last week.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what do we do?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We could make something at home.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: With what? We don't have any food.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We could eat the alphabet soup... without the soup.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's just letters, Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have some expired yogurt in my fridge.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How expired?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Perfect! That's a 1997 vintage yogurt!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You know what my fantasy is? That you talk like a normal person.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just delivered a pretentious Fantasy Island monologue about rekindling a stranger's love
jokes.punchline: Chandler cuts through all the romanticism to wish Ross just spoke normally
jokes.explanation: A very strong Chandler line. The structure is elegant: Ross set up a 'my fantasy is...' frame, and Chandler hijacks the exact same frame to deflate it entirely. High character integration — this is peak Chandler as the self-aware deflator of Ross's pretension. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I got the job! I'm the new lunch chef at Bloomingdale's!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know! And if I didn't get it, why would I even be telling you this story?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Oh, my God. You are pure evil.' / Ross: 'Okay, pure evil... horny and alone.'
jokes.setup: Chandler accuses Ross of being 'pure evil' for his plan to intercept Jade from a blind date
jokes.punchline: Ross accepts the 'pure evil' label but immediately qualifies it with 'horny and alone' — self-aware pathos that gets a laugh
jokes.explanation: Strong exchange. Ross's self-amendment of 'pure evil' to 'pure evil, horny and alone' is the show at its best: character-driven comedy where the punchline also generates sympathy. The economy of the revision is excellent — three words that reframe everything.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We should do something special to celebrate your promotion!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, we could go to that fancy restaurant downtown.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That place is really expensive though.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I could sell one of my kidneys.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, no!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? I have two of them. I only need one.

jokes.text: Chandler quietly says 'I've done this.' after Ross describes the predatory scheme
jokes.setup: Ross has outlined a morally dubious plan to pick up a woman who was stood up by 'Bob'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's soft, matter-of-fact 'I've done this.' — confessing to the same behavior with no shame or elaboration
jokes.explanation: Three words and maximum laugh. The economy here is nearly perfect. Chandler's admission functions as both a punchline to Ross's scheme and a character revelation delivered with complete deadpan. The scene marker suggests a pause/beat before this line, which would make it land even harder in performance.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, I know Bob stood you up, but don't worry. He's just going through a really sensitive time right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Here, have a tissue.

jokes.text: Monica: 'While Ross is on the phone, everybody owes me 62 bucks for his birthday.' Joey: 'Is there any chance you're rounding up from... like 20?'
jokes.setup: Monica announces everyone owes $62 for Ross's birthday
jokes.punchline: Joey asks if she's rounding up 'from like 20?' — revealing the gap between what he has and what's being asked, with his hopeful tone making it funnier
jokes.explanation: A clean character joke — Joey's financial naivety and broke status are well-established, and 'from like 20?' captures his optimistic cluelessness perfectly. Sets up the episode's economic divide theme.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Here, take a tissue.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, I think you've hit your daily crying quota.

jokes.text: Phoebe repeats 'It's Ross' in a flat tone mimicking Monica's earnest appeal, then immediately says 'See you later. I gotta go... do a thing!'
jokes.setup: Monica has justified the $62 cost by saying 'But it's Ross' with great feeling; the others echo it
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's flat echo of 'It's Ross' undercuts the sentiment, then she immediately bolts with the paper-thin excuse 'do a thing' — clearly fleeing the bill
jokes.explanation: The joke has two beats — the hollow echo and the flight. Both work independently but together create a nice escalation. Phoebe's vague 'do a thing' is a classic deflection gag that's relatable and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And the best part? I get my own beeper!

jokes.text: Joey: 'Well, I gotta start saving up for Ross' birthday.' / Rachel: 'I guess I'll just stay home and eat dust bunnies.'
jokes.setup: The group is figuring out dinner plans after the $62 birthday bomb
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'eat dust bunnies' — a genuinely bleak image of poverty delivered with her trademark dramatic flair
jokes.explanation: 'Eat dust bunnies' is a memorably specific image for poverty — funnier than 'eat nothing' and more visual. Joey's straight-faced savings plan also gets a small laugh before Rachel's escalation lands.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: These prices are insane! What, the chickens must be celebrities or something?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, like 'Chicken Denise Richards' – she costs extra.

jokes.text: 'If it's not you, this is a horrible story.'
jokes.setup: Monica is building up to a big work announcement — 'Leon called me into his office...'
jokes.punchline: Chandler interrupts with 'If it's not you, this is a horrible story' — meta-commentary on the storytelling convention of a tease before good news
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines — and arguably one of the most Chandler lines ever written. It's meta-comedic (commenting on Monica's storytelling structure), perfectly economical, and completely character-specific. Chandler's deflation of dramatic builds is his comedic DNA. The line is highly quotable and has real-world applicability. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me you've been pretending to be someone else this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: This is like Three's Company!

jokes.text: Monica announces 'I think we should go out and celebrate. Someplace nice.' — then cut to Rachel and Joey mouthing 'Someplace nice' to each other in dread
jokes.setup: The three broke friends have just been complaining about expensive outings; Monica arrives with great news
jokes.punchline: Monica uses the exact phrase ('someplace nice') the friends were dreading, and their reaction beat sells the irony
jokes.explanation: Strong structural callback — the phrase 'someplace nice' was seeded in the previous scene and lands here as dramatic irony. The visual beat of Joey and Rachel mouthing it to each other is the payoff. Earns its laughs through setup, not randomness.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Ordering expensive Thai chicken pizza... hoping that removing ingredients will reduce the already high price

jokes.text: Joey: 'How much you think I can get for my kidney?'
jokes.setup: The broke friends are staring down another expensive dinner at 'someplace nice'
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately pivots to organ sales as a financial solution — the absurdity of the leap and his earnest delivery is the joke
jokes.explanation: A darkly funny line that works because of Joey's earnestness. He's not being sarcastic — he genuinely considers this. That sincerity is what makes it a character joke rather than a random dark joke. Economical and memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: What would the side salad be on the side of?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: On the side of my plate.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: No, I mean what would it be a side to?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! On the side of my water glass.

jokes.text: Ross's moral plea to himself: 'We don't know Bob. We know me. We like me. Please let me be happy.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to get Ross to do the right thing — not steal Jade from Bob
jokes.punchline: Ross's self-advocacy collapses into a pathetic 'Please let me be happy' — the emotional nakedness of a grown man pleading for romantic permission
jokes.explanation: A great cringe-comedy beat that generates both laughs and sympathy. The escalation from 'We don't know Bob' (reasonable) to 'Please let me be happy' (nakedly pathetic) is well-calibrated. The switch from third-person 'we' to first-person pleading is a nice structural touch. Very Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'll have the cucumber soup.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I'm outta here!

jokes.text: Ross goes to confess to Jade; instead of confessing says 'Whoever stood you up is a jerk' and plays the comforting stranger
jokes.setup: Chandler has pushed Ross to go confess the truth to Jade
jokes.punchline: Ross completely abandons the confession and instead plays the role of sympathetic stranger — pretending NOT to be the person who didn't show up
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe beat — the audience watches Ross do the exact opposite of what he promised. The irony of him calling 'Bob' a jerk while being Bob-adjacent is the comedic core. Carries through on the episode's premise nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Can you sing 'Happy Birthday' for us?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: Sure thing!

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Actually, on second thought... just wash your hands first.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I just had this weird sense. But that's me, I'm weird and sensitive.'
jokes.setup: Jade asks how Ross knew she was stood up
jokes.punchline: Ross leans into a fake sensitive-guy persona to impress her — 'weird and sensitive' is meant to be charming but reads as slightly pathetic
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — Ross trying too hard to seem sensitive while being entirely insensitive in his actions. The irony does the work, but the line itself is fairly generic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh come on, we always split the bill equally!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, that was $300! I didn't even eat half of that!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This is exactly like prom night when Brad said he'd pay and then—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, Brad ditched you on prom?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, but he made everyone split his corsage cost, and it was humiliating!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is... financial betrayal at fancy events runs in your life?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Technically, this is worse because we're all adults and should know better.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, at least at prom you could blame hormones. This is just sad.

jokes.text: Ross offers Jade a tissue and says 'No, you keep the pack. I'm all cried out today.'
jokes.setup: Ross is performing sensitive stranger while consoling Jade
jokes.punchline: 'I'm all cried out today' — a casual admission that he's been crying all day, ostensibly over Julie, which he deploys as a bonding moment
jokes.explanation: A quietly excellent line. The fact that Ross has genuinely been crying all day (over Julie) makes this accidentally true, which adds a layer to the comedy. He's accidentally sharing real emotional vulnerability while trying to fake sensitivity. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So... how's everyone doing? Good? Great.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why do you sound like you're about to tell us someone died?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No one died. I just... we've noticed that when we all go out, there's this thing that happens.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What thing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The... the money thing. Some of us have more of it than others, and it gets weird.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Are you calling me poor?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's being very diplomatic about it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, maybe we should be more... aware. Of different... financial situations.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm not offended. I've been poor, I've been rich—well, I've been poor.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This is incredibly awkward.

jokes.text: Monica's promotion toast keeps getting interrupted with addendums: 'Head lunch chef... also in charge of purchasing... who has her own little desk when Roland's not there'
jokes.setup: Friends are toasting Monica's promotion; each time someone starts the toast, she adds another detail to her title
jokes.punchline: The title keeps diminishing with each qualifier — 'when Roland's not there' undercuts all previous grandeur
jokes.explanation: A well-crafted escalating bit with each interruption diminishing the previous grandeur. The structure is perfect — each addendum reveals the promotion is slightly less impressive than stated, culminating in 'when Roland's not there' which deflates the whole thing. Monica's earnestness against the increasingly underwhelming details is perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. There was going to be a hoopla?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: For me?

jokes.text: 'Wait! And I got a beeper!' — Monica adds a beeper to her toast credentials
jokes.setup: The toast has already been deflated by 'when Roland's not there'
jokes.punchline: Monica interrupts again to add 'And I got a beeper!' — the beeper being the final, supremely underwhelming credential
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the toast sequence. The beeper is the peak of anti-climax — in 1995, beepers were borderline cool, making this a perfectly calibrated deflation. Chandler's 'That's fine, I'll just wait' in response is the cherry on top. Monica's sincere pride in the beeper is what makes it land — she genuinely thinks this is impressive, which is pure character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So... leprosy. Am I right?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'That's fine, I'll just wait.' — in response to Monica interrupting the toast again
jokes.setup: The toast has been interrupted multiple times; Chandler was in mid-sentence when Monica cut in with the beeper
jokes.punchline: Chandler's weary 'That's fine, I'll just wait' — maximum patience signaling maximum exasperation
jokes.explanation: Another economical Chandler reaction that does a lot with little. The weary resignation is perfectly timed as a button to the interruption gag. Classic Chandler long-suffering straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, I have something very special for you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh Monica, you shouldn't have!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But I did! *dramatically opens box* Behold!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: *gasps theatrically* It's... it's beautiful!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, we get it. You guys are doing the thing.

jokes.text: Waiter: 'Are we ready to order?' Group: 'We haven't even looked yet.' Waiter: 'When you do, let me know. I'll be over there on the edge of my seat.'
jokes.setup: The group hasn't looked at the menu; the waiter checks in
jokes.punchline: The waiter's sarcastic 'I'll be over there on the edge of my seat' — passive-aggressive restaurant humor delivered drily
jokes.explanation: A solid one-liner from a minor character. The waiter's sarcasm is a reliable comedic device but it's not particularly fresh. Works as a scene-setting gag for the restaurant sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We practiced this bit, and it felt a lot less dorky in rehearsal.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Yeah, these are pretty "cha-ching"'
jokes.setup: The group is staring at the expensive menu
jokes.punchline: 'Cha-ching' as a descriptor for expensive — Rachel's upscale-but-broke character using a cash-register sound effect as an adjective
jokes.explanation: A light gag — the onomatopoeia as adjective is mildly clever. Character-appropriate for Rachel who bridges the worlds of wealth-familiarity and current poverty. Not exceptional but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, we could always use the extra seats to display our collection of fancy hats.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Or we could just... sell them.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Where's the fun in that?

jokes.text: Monica: 'I know! What are these, famous chickens?'
jokes.setup: The group has just noted the high prices on the menu
jokes.punchline: 'What are these, famous chickens?' — implying the chicken dishes are so expensive they must be celebrity birds
jokes.explanation: A genuinely good line. 'Famous chickens' is specific enough to be funny — it conjures an absurd image and is the kind of throwaway line that sticks in memory. Works as an observational gag with a light absurdist twist.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Casually adding major life update as if it's routine preparation

jokes.text: Monica: 'Tell me again. What do I do when Mr. Roper calls?'
jokes.setup: Ross has just explained the phone number confusion chain
jokes.punchline: Monica sarcastically invokes Mr. Roper from Three's Company — a show built around exactly this kind of identity confusion/misunderstanding premise
jokes.explanation: A smart pop-culture reference that actually earns its place — the Three's Company comparison is apt (identity-swapping confusion) not random. Monica calling out that she's living in a sitcom within a sitcom gives it a slight meta quality. Economical and well-landed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You had sex today?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You had sex today?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You had sex today?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah!

jokes.text: Joey orders the Thai chicken pizza 'without the nuts and leeks and stuff' hoping it will be cheaper — waiter: 'You'd think, wouldn't you?'
jokes.setup: Joey is ordering from an expensive menu and tries to budget by removing expensive ingredients
jokes.punchline: The waiter's 'You'd think, wouldn't you?' — confirming the restaurant's extortion while offering no help
jokes.explanation: The waiter's line is the gem here. 'You'd think, wouldn't you?' is a perfect four-word expression of restaurant capitalism — confirming the absurdity without doing anything about it. Character-specific for Joey who genuinely thought he found a loophole.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't need to screen my calls anymore. I'm having sex.

jokes.text: Rachel orders 'the side salad' / Waiter: 'And what would that be on the side of?' / Rachel: 'Just put it right here next to my water.'
jokes.setup: Rachel, clearly trying to save money, orders a side salad as her entire meal
jokes.punchline: The waiter's technically correct question ('what would that be on the side of?') and Rachel's defeated 'just put it right here next to my water' expose the poverty of her dinner
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The waiter's pedantic literalism ('what would that be on the side of?') is genuinely clever — a side salad requires a main. Rachel's deflated 'just put it right here next to my water' is a perfect punchline that conveys dignity-in-poverty. The whole exchange is tightly constructed and highly relatable. Earns 8+ for the elegant structure and the layered character moment.

jokes.text: Phoebe orders Cajun catfish then asks for 'a verse of Killing Me Softly' — threatens the waiter's fish if he sneezes
jokes.setup: Phoebe orders her food; the waiter completes the order and asks 'Anything else?'
jokes.punchline: 'Yes, how about a verse of Killing Me Softly?' — then pre-emptively warns: 'You're gonna sneeze in my fish, aren't you?'
jokes.explanation: Reliably Phoebe-ish absurdism — the song request feels random but Phoebe's intuition about the waiter sneezing is the better gag. Two beats that work together to characterize her as a benevolent eccentric.

dialogue.speaker: Jade
dialogue.line: And then he just... finished. Like, thirty seconds in. I've had longer commercial breaks.

dialogue.speaker: Jade
dialogue.line: The whole thing was awkward. You kept bumping your head on the headboard, you were sweating everywhere, and honestly, I'm not even sure you knew where anything was.

dialogue.speaker: Jade
dialogue.line: Two out of ten. And that's only because I'm being generous.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You're gonna sneeze in my fish, aren't you?'
jokes.setup: After Chandler's sarcastic song request, the waiter (presumably) gives him a look
jokes.punchline: Chandler pre-emptively acknowledges the retaliation he's invited — a paranoid but logical conclusion
jokes.explanation: A great quick beat. The specificity of imagining the waiter's revenge (sneezing in his fish) and Chandler's resigned delivery makes this a solid follow-up to the song bit.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Monica? Wow, it's been so long! How have you been?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Stevie! Oh my God, look at you! You're all grown up!

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Yeah, well... So, uh, how well did you know my dad back then?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? Your dad? I mean, I knew him as your father. Why?

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: No reason, just... did he ever try anything weird with you?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: WHAT?!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Woah! Does anybody else feel like they just gave birth to an alien?' — reacting to the bill
jokes.setup: The bill arrives after the expensive dinner
jokes.punchline: Phoebe describes the bill shock with the alien birth metaphor — visceral, specific, and uniquely Phoebe
jokes.explanation: A great Phoebe line — the 'gave birth to an alien' metaphor for financial shock is wonderfully specific and weird. Only Phoebe would describe sticker shock this way, making it high on character integration. The absurdity is earned because it's grounded in a real physical sensation (gut-punch of a big bill).

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It was Blowfish.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The band?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: Ross starts to split the bill six ways, Monica says don't count herself — 'Oh! You're right, I'm sorry. It's Monica's big night. She shouldn't pay.' Then: 'So five of us is... 33.50 a piece.'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to divide the check equally; Monica's night means she doesn't pay
jokes.punchline: The 'generous' gesture of not charging Monica actually makes it MORE expensive for everyone else — the math joke lands as a sad escalation
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the math — the generous gesture backfires. Standard sitcom escalation but well-timed. The pause before '33.50' suggests a beat of Ross doing the calculation, which would play well in performance.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: You guys were all out having fun while I stayed home alone!

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: You know what I did? I played this weird game where I guessed which finger you were thinking of.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: And I won. Every. Single. Time.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Prom night flashback.'
jokes.setup: The trio is about to be forced to pay $33.50 each for food they didn't really eat
jokes.punchline: 'Prom night flashback' — a single phrase that implies she was exploited or overcharged at prom, delivered with absolute Phoebe calm
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous laugh. 'Prom night flashback' is a masterclass in economy — it implies a whole backstory (Phoebe's difficult youth, being taken advantage of) without explaining anything. The gap between what's implied and what's said IS the joke. Perfect character integration — this throwaway line hints at Phoebe's rough past without dwelling on it. One of the episode's best jokes and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So I'm talking to the lead singer of the band, and he's really charming, and I'm laughing at all his jokes...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And then what happened?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, he leaned in and gave me a hickey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A hickey? From the lead singer? That's awesome!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, that's so unlike you!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hickeys are just marks of passion, you know?

jokes.text: Phoebe's speech: 'Rachel just had that little salad... and Joey with his teeny pizza!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is breaking the social contract by refusing to split evenly
jokes.punchline: The framing of the food as 'little salad' and 'teeny pizza' — the diminutive adjectives make the injustice of even-splitting viscerally clear
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Phoebe being the one to break the social omertà about money at dinner. 'Teeny pizza' is a good specific detail. Functions as both a comedy beat and the pivot into the episode's thematic conflict.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: I'll buy your coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Can I borrow twenty bucks?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Yeah, hello? It's us. We'll be fine.'
jokes.setup: The broke trio hesitates to raise the money issue; the richer trio urges them to speak up
jokes.punchline: 'It's us. We'll be fine.' — dramatic irony because they will very much NOT be fine; the confidence is immediately undercut by what follows
jokes.explanation: More functional than funny — the irony plays out in retrospect when they do NOT handle it fine. A setup beat more than a joke on its own, but it earns a rewatch bonus because the dramatic irony lands better on repeat viewings.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I guess I just never think of money as an issue.' Chandler: 'Because you have it.' Ross: 'Good point!'
jokes.setup: Ross admits he doesn't think of money as an issue
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry clarification 'Because you have it' — stating the obvious with maximum flatness; Ross's genuine 'Good point!' reveals he hadn't even considered this
jokes.explanation: A sharp exchange — Chandler's reduction of Ross's clueless wealth-privilege to three words is excellent. What makes it better is Ross's genuine 'Good point!' — he truly hadn't made this connection, revealing both his obliviousness and his good nature. Strong economy throughout.

jokes.text: The Hootie and the Blowfish reveal — Ross didn't know the concert was the gift; thought there'd be a 'hoopla' separately
jokes.setup: The birthday financial conflict is being aired; someone mentions 'the hoopla'
jokes.punchline: Ross didn't know the concert WAS the gift — 'Gift? The thing's not the gift?' — his confusion reveals everyone has been agonizing over a plan he didn't even understand
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — all the financial anxiety was over something the honoree didn't even understand. The gap between what people suffered through and what Ross expected is the comedic engine. Functions well as both a joke and a plot complication.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'If it makes anybody feel better, forget the thing and we'll just do the gift.' Joey: 'Gift? The thing's not the gift?'
jokes.setup: The Hootie concert confusion is unfolding — everyone assumed everyone else understood the plan
jokes.punchline: Joey separately didn't know either — a second character reveals equal confusion, doubling the joke
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from discovering a second person was equally confused — Joey's echo of the same misunderstanding escalates the absurdity. Good character work: of course Joey also didn't know.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Hootie and the... I can catch them on the radio.'
jokes.setup: The concert is revealed as a gift; the financial burden is discussed; Joey is trying to seem unbothered
jokes.punchline: 'I can catch them on the radio' — Joey's breezy dismissal of a major concert gift, performed as if this is a completely reasonable alternative
jokes.explanation: A nice deflation joke — dismissing a concert by saying you can hear them on the radio captures both Joey's working-class pragmatism and the slightly sad reality of the financial divide. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'So, the Ebola virus. That's gotta suck, huh?'
jokes.setup: After the emotionally charged money conversation, there is an enormous silence at the dinner table
jokes.punchline: Chandler attempts to break the silence with the most jarring possible small talk topic: the Ebola virus
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a strong candidate for all-time Friends moments. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) The awkward silence is painfully established; (2) Chandler's instinct is to break tension but he's so bad at it that he leads with a deadly virus; (3) The tonal whiplash from emotional confrontation to Ebola small talk is enormous; (4) 'That's gotta suck, huh?' is the perfect colloquial understatement for a hemorrhagic fever. Totally character-specific — Chandler is the chaos agent of awkward silences. Highly quotable, highly rewatchable. This is a 8+ joke.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'By the way, this didn't seem so dorky out in the hall.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler have staged a little 'skit' to present the steaks and concert tickets
jokes.punchline: Chandler breaks the skit to acknowledge it was poorly conceived — but only AFTER going through with it
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler self-awareness line — the joke is that he committed to the skit, it was clearly dorky, and he can only comment after the fact. The 'out in the hall' detail suggests they rehearsed it, making the self-critique funnier. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Joey signals with fingers how small the charity makes them feel — 'Actually, it makes us feel that big.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe says the gesture makes them feel 'about this big' — signaling a small amount with fingers
jokes.punchline: Joey corrects downward — 'Actually, it makes us feel THAT big' — an even smaller finger gap, a visual gag implying even more diminished
jokes.explanation: A nice visual gag escalation — the finger-gap metric for feelings is funny on its own, and Joey undercutting Phoebe's already small measurement extends the joke well. Economy of the visual punchline is high.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I'm just not in a very "Hootie" place right now.'
jokes.setup: After the emotional argument, Phoebe refuses to go to the concert
jokes.punchline: 'Not in a very Hootie place right now' — using 'Hootie' as an emotional/spiritual state, a perfectly Phoebe-ized version of refusing an invitation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Phoebe lines. Treating a pop band as an emotional/spiritual state ('Hootie place') is completely in character and completely absurd at the same time. Only Phoebe would speak this way. Highly quotable — applicable well beyond this episode. The economy of the phrase is excellent. Earns 8+ for the perfect character integration and the freshness of the concept.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Then you'll have extra seats for all your tiaras and stuff.'
jokes.setup: The wealthier trio says 'We bought the tickets' implying the broke trio should still go
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's exit line — 'all your tiaras and stuff' — a royalty metaphor for the richer friends that's petty and funny
jokes.explanation: A good exit line — the tiaras imagery is unexpected and funny. Using 'tiaras and stuff' to characterize wealthy friends as royalty is an absurd but well-calibrated insult. The 'and stuff' throwaway at the end is a nice casual touch.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Why did you look at me when you said that?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe said 'tiaras and stuff' while presumably looking directly at Chandler (who is the most effeminate/fussy of the wealthy trio)
jokes.punchline: Chandler's wounded protest — he's been silently targeted by the tiara comment and needs it acknowledged
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the tiara joke. Chandler asking why he was looked at implies he understands why — the self-aware protest makes the subtext text. Economy is near-perfect: nine words that say everything. A great visual gag payoff to Phoebe's insult.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Just let me grab my jacket and tell you I had sex today.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks if Chandler is ready to go to the concert
jokes.punchline: He tacks 'and tell you I had sex today' onto the mundane jacket-grabbing task — the casual delivery of huge personal news as an afterthought
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top three jokes. The structure is genius: 'let me grab my jacket' sets up a totally mundane action, making 'and tell you I had sex today' a maximum-impact non sequitur. The casual equivalence of grabbing a jacket and announcing sex is perfectly Chandler — he can't just say it, he has to bury it in a list. High economy, perfect character integration. Monica's double-take is implied and beautiful.

jokes.text: Monica: 'What? You had sex today?' Chandler: 'It sounds even cooler when somebody else says it!'
jokes.setup: Monica reacts with shock to Chandler's sex announcement
jokes.punchline: 'It sounds even cooler when somebody else says it!' — Chandler is so delighted by the echo of his own news that he validates Monica's reaction as an enhancement
jokes.explanation: Exceptional follow-up to an already great joke. The callback structure — Chandler's announcement → Monica's reaction → Chandler enjoying the echo — is a three-beat escalation that all pays off. 'It sounds even cooler when somebody else says it' is quotable beyond the episode. Strong character work: Chandler's sex life is so rare he savors the announcement itself.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I was awesome. She was biting her lip to stop from screaming.' — delivered with maximum pride
jokes.setup: The sex announcement has landed; Chandler begins to detail the encounter
jokes.punchline: 'She was biting her lip to stop from screaming' — presented as a triumph; the detail will become the punchline of the later phone message
jokes.explanation: This line functions primarily as setup for the later phone message payoff, but it also works as a standalone character beat — Chandler's pride in what he believes to be his sexual prowess. The rewatch bonus is very high because this line gets funnier retroactively.

jokes.text: Chandler still screening calls: 'I had sex today. / I never have to answer that phone again.'
jokes.setup: Earlier, Chandler was screening calls to seem like he had a life
jokes.punchline: Now that he's had sex, he recasts the phone screening — he's ACTUALLY got something better to do. 'I never have to answer that phone again.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback to the phone screening setup from the cold open. The original joke was Chandler screening to seem like he had a life; now he ironically HAS a life event worth missing calls for. The escalation from fake coolness to genuine cool is a satisfying structural arc. 'I never have to answer that phone again' is overstated to perfection.

jokes.text: Jade's voicemail reveals she had sex with 'the guy' she met — Ross listens; 'Bob here.'
jokes.setup: Jade is leaving a message for Bob; Ross is listening and impersonating Bob
jokes.punchline: The immediate 'Bob here' pickup — Ross can't help himself again, exactly like the cold open; perfect structural callback
jokes.explanation: A structural callback to the episode's best early joke. The exact same mechanism (screening calls, then picking up for Jade) fires again, but with dramatically higher stakes — now we know Ross slept with her, she's calling to report on it to 'Bob,' and Ross has to hear it. The callback earns its repeat by amplifying the cringe and irony. Strong rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Ross as Bob asks Jade 'So how was he?' about himself
jokes.setup: Jade has revealed she had sex with a guy she met (Ross); Ross, pretending to be Bob, asks her to evaluate the encounter
jokes.punchline: He asks 'So how was he?' — setting himself up to hear his own sexual review delivered to someone else
jokes.explanation: Brilliant cringe setup. The question 'so how was he?' is Ross asking for a performance review of himself in the third person — an act of both ego and masochism. The audience knows what's coming (bad news) making the tension delicious. One of the strongest structural jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Jade: 'Oh Bob, he was nothing compared to you.' — completely deflating Chandler's proud account
jokes.setup: Chandler bragged that the woman bit her lip to stop from screaming
jokes.punchline: Jade tells 'Bob' the sex was 'nothing compared' to Bob — meaning Chandler, who thought he was amazing, was NOT
jokes.explanation: The payoff of a beautifully constructed delayed callback. Chandler's proud boast about the lip-biting is completely demolished by Jade's verdict — delivered unknowingly to the very man she's critiquing. The structure is exceptional: setup 15 minutes earlier, payoff now, and the person being discussed is listening. Very strong craft score for the structure alone.

jokes.text: Jade: 'I bit my lip to keep from screaming your name.' — i.e., screaming 'Bob' not in pleasure but as a reflex
jokes.setup: Chandler claimed the lip-biting was because she was overwhelmed with pleasure; now Jade reveals to 'Bob' she was biting her lip to suppress screaming a DIFFERENT name
jokes.punchline: The lip-biting was to suppress screaming for Bob — not from pleasure with Chandler, but from longing for someone else during the act
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's crown jewel of structure. The lip-biting detail from Chandler's boast is completely recontextualized: she wasn't biting her lip because she was overwhelmed by Chandler — she was biting it to stop herself from calling out Bob's name. The inversion is devastating, perfectly timed, and completely earned. The same physical detail means two opposite things. This is sophisticated comedy writing. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Jade: 'It was just so awkward and bumpy.' Ross: 'Maybe he had some kind of new style you're not familiar with.'
jokes.setup: Jade is describing the sex negatively; Ross is listening as 'Bob'
jokes.punchline: Ross, in full cringe mode, defends himself in the third person by suggesting his terrible technique was actually 'a new style'
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy — Ross cannot stop himself from defending his own sexual performance while pretending to be someone else. 'A new style you're not familiar with' is the perfect cope, and the fact that he delivers it while hearing it described as 'awkward and bumpy' makes it even better. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jade: 'There wasn't much time to get used to it... if you know what I mean.'
jokes.setup: Ross suggested Jade just needed time to get used to his 'new style'
jokes.punchline: Jade's 'there wasn't much time to get used to it, if you know what I mean' — a delicate way of saying Chandler was quick, which devastates him further
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly understated punchline. 'There wasn't much time to get used to it, if you know what I mean' is the politest possible way to accuse someone of premature ejaculation, and delivered to the man himself (through the Bob fiction) it's maximally devastating. The primness of the delivery ('if you know what I mean') amplifies the cruelty. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Jade: '...there wasn't much time to get used to it, if you know what I mean.'
jokes.setup: Chandler-as-Bob defends the mysterious man's 'new style' and says she needs to get used to it
jokes.punchline: Jade implies it was over very quickly — a double-barreled insult (awkward AND fast)
jokes.explanation: The 'not much time to get used to it' lands well as escalation of the humiliation. Effective use of implication rather than explicit statement, which is the right call.

jokes.text: Ross: 'You know what? I'm not gonna be able to enjoy this.' (decides to go to the concert)
jokes.setup: Ross has just learned he was terrible in bed and finished quickly, via his own fake Bob phone call
jokes.punchline: His understated 'I'm not gonna be able to enjoy this' — a massive understatement for the psychological damage he just sustained
jokes.explanation: Good button to the Jade phone call sequence. The understatement of 'I'm not gonna be able to enjoy this' for what was basically a sexual humiliation delivered in real-time is perfectly calibrated. Ross's resignation rather than rage is a nice character choice.

jokes.text: The rich trio at the concert: 'Well, maybe we should stay for one song. It would be rude to leave.' — they're clearly having a great time
jokes.setup: The wealthier trio went to the concert despite the fight; they feel guilty about their broke friends
jokes.punchline: Their transparent rationalization for staying ('it would be rude to them') when they're clearly loving it — performative guilt vs. actual guilt
jokes.explanation: Standard dramatic irony — the audience sees through their rationalization. Functional but not particularly crafted. Sets up the hickey reveal nicely.

jokes.text: After concert — 'Amazing! Excellent! I can't believe the guys missed it! What guys? Oh, yeah.'
jokes.setup: The trio returns from the concert obviously having had a great time
jokes.punchline: One of them briefly forgets their broke friends exist — 'What guys? Oh, yeah.' — guilt immediately following amnesia
jokes.explanation: 'What guys? Oh, yeah.' is a small but effective joke — in the euphoria of the concert, they momentarily forgot about the drama. The beat of remembering is the joke. Economy is the strength here.

jokes.text: Monica encounters her former babysitting charge Stevie Fisher, now a lawyer: 'You can't be a lawyer. You're 8.'
jokes.setup: Monica runs into a kid she once babysat; he tells her he's now a lawyer
jokes.punchline: 'You can't be a lawyer. You're 8.' — Monica's brain failing to update her mental image of him
jokes.explanation: A solid quick joke — 'You can't be a lawyer. You're 8.' is the natural comedic response and it lands well. The delivery in performance would elevate it; on the page it's functional. Sets up the Blowfish access joke nicely.

jokes.text: Stevie Fisher: 'My firm represents the band. You guys wanna meet the group?' / Monica: 'Are you one of the ones that fooled around with my dad?'
jokes.setup: Little Stevie has backstage access to Hootie; Monica and friends are thrilled
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately asks Stevie if he's one of the Blowfish who slept with her father — an insane detail delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: A genuinely surprising joke — the Hootie/dad connection comes from nowhere and is delivered with complete casualness, which is the key. The absurdity of the detail (Monica's father slept with a Blowfish) combined with her practical need to know creates a great dark-comedy beat. The '90s specificity makes it a fun period piece.

jokes.text: 'Is that a hickey?' / 'Oh, no, I just... I fell down.' / 'On someone's lips?'
jokes.setup: Monica has a visible hickey from the Hootie backstage party; she tries to deny it
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'On someone's lips?' — the perfect comic response to an obviously terrible lie
jokes.explanation: 'On someone's lips?' is an economical and effective punchline — the absurd logic of 'falling on lips' is dissected with a single question. Joey's confusion-as-wit is always good character work. Economy is the standout quality.

jokes.text: Monica's increasingly vague 'party / gathering of people / with food and music / and the band'
jokes.setup: Monica is being caught in her lie about not having fun the previous night
jokes.punchline: Each vague synonym she uses (party → gathering → food and music) only confirms the truth; 'and the band' is the final self-incriminating reveal
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed escalating confession — each attempt to minimize reveals more. 'And the band' as the final incriminating detail is perfectly landed. The structure mirrors the toast sequence's escalating reveal technique used earlier.

jokes.text: Monica's increasingly elaborate hickey explanation: 'It wasn't a party so much as a... gathering of people... with food and music and... and the band.'
jokes.setup: Monica is asked where she got the hickey; she starts with 'I fell down,' then is pushed to admit it was a party
jokes.punchline: Her sentence keeps extending with qualifiers that incrementally reveal she was at the concert, culminating in 'and the band' — which gives everything away
jokes.explanation: A well-structured escalating confession. The comedic rhythm of adding detail after detail — each one making it worse — is classic farce construction. 'And the band' is the perfect final reveal.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Who gave you that hickey?' Monica: 'That would be the work of a Blowfish.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks directly who gave Monica the hickey
jokes.punchline: 'That would be the work of a Blowfish.' — the band name doing double comic duty as literal description
jokes.explanation: The episode's most quotable joke. 'That would be the work of a Blowfish' is constructed perfectly — the formality of 'that would be the work of' makes the absurd reveal funnier, and the wordplay between 'blowfish' (the animal, relevant to hickeys) and the band name is clean and well-earned. Maximum economy, huge crowd reaction. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Joey: 'I can't believe it! We're just sitting at home, trying to guess Joey's fingers...'
jokes.setup: Joey erupts at learning the others partied with Hootie
jokes.punchline: 'Trying to guess Joey's fingers' — in outrage, he reveals their humble evening's entertainment was guessing how many fingers he was holding up
jokes.explanation: A great throwaway detail that generates a big laugh. 'Guess Joey's fingers' implies they were so bored they played children's games with each other — and the specific image of guessing fingers (not even a real game) is perfectly pathetic. Character-specific: Joey would both be the proposer and subject of this game.

jokes.text: Joey: '...and you're partying and having fun and all: "Hey, Blowfish, suck on my neck!"'
jokes.setup: Joey is ranting about the others partying with Hootie while they sat home
jokes.punchline: Joey's imagined version of events — Monica enthusiastically soliciting hickeys from band members — delivered with outraged disgust
jokes.explanation: Joey's dramatized version of the night — 'Hey, Blowfish, suck on my neck!' — is both a callback to the hickey reveal and a great character moment. Joey's outrage expressed through increasingly absurd imagined scenarios is peak Joey. The delivery implied by the caps is essential.

jokes.text: Chandler/Ross/Monica: 'Don't blame us. You could've been there.' / Joey/Phoebe: 'What? As part of your "poor friends outreach program"?'
jokes.setup: The wealthier friends defend themselves by saying the broke trio could have come
jokes.punchline: 'Poor friends outreach program' — a perfectly sharp coinage for the dynamic they've been fighting all episode
jokes.explanation: 'Poor friends outreach program' is a great coinage — it crystallizes the entire episode's economic tension into a three-word institutional metaphor. The formality of 'outreach program' against the personal context is the comedic engine. Sharp writing.

jokes.text: Monica's pager goes off mid-argument — she steps away; it's work calling about the steaks
jokes.setup: The beeper was introduced as a symbol of Monica's promotion ('And I got a beeper!')
jokes.punchline: The beeper fires at the worst possible moment — during a fight — and the call is bad news (the steak kickback investigation)
jokes.explanation: A structural callback to the beeper as a symbol of success — now it's delivering failure. The reversal is elegantly plotted. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing, the pride in the beeper becomes sadder and funnier simultaneously.

jokes.text: Monica: 'I just got fired.' — delivered with complete flatness after the phone call
jokes.setup: Monica stepped away from the fight to take a work call; the group waited
jokes.punchline: 'I just got fired.' — maximum understatement for a massive personal catastrophe, delivered in the middle of a friend fight
jokes.explanation: Four words that hit harder for being so understated. The timing — mid-fight, after the beeper moment — makes the flatness funnier and sadder. Monica's flat delivery of catastrophic news is excellent character work (her need to maintain composure). The irony of the episode's inciting celebration turning to termination is sharp plotting.

jokes.text: Final diner scene — 'Here's your check. That'll be $4.12.' / 'Let me get that.' / 'You got 5 bucks?'
jokes.setup: The entire episode has been about economic inequality among the friends
jokes.punchline: The final check is $4.12 — a diner bill — and the formerly rich friends now have to ask for a $5 contribution. The role reversal/leveling is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed structural joke that closes the episode's thematic arc. The $4.12 diner bill vs. the $33-per-person fancy restaurant bill is the whole episode in miniature. Monica offering to pay then needing to borrow a $5 is the perfect visual punctuation mark on the money storyline. Strong for structure and thematic payoff.

jokes.text: Final voicemail tag — Jade leaving another message for 'Bob', describing 'one hot, steamy, wild night' after everything Ross heard
jokes.setup: Ross has heard Jade's assessment of their encounter (awkward, bumpy, quick); now Jade is leaving another flirty message for Bob
jokes.punchline: Jade is obliviously describing to 'Bob' what she wants — a 'hot, steamy, wild night' — after just telling Bob (Ross) the sex was terrible. The dramatic irony of her continued pursuit creates the cringe
jokes.explanation: A solid tag that leaves the storyline on a cringe-funny note. Jade still pursuing 'Bob' after effectively telling him the sex was bad creates good ironic closure. The episode ends on a laugh without fully resolving the comic situation — a smart choice.

tmdb_overview: When a sexy woman calls the wrong number, Chandler seeks to make the most of the situation. Income issues divide the friends; Monica, Ross and Chandler have money, while Phoebe, Rachel and Joey don't.
insight: Five steaks episode underperforms at 70.9 despite character-comedy strength and escalating tension.
